CHAPTER XI

Tame and Wild Packet Geometry

For local Langlands





Mathematical text





Komorebi P.

Abstract. Let K be a nonarchimedean local field. We resolve several finite layers that occur inside the local
Langlands correspondence for general linear groups. Frobenius semisimple Weil Deligne parameters first
split into irreducible Weil atoms and finite monodromy chains. In the tame case, character projectors show
that every irreducible atom is one transitive Frobenius orbit, and Mackey theory gives an exact greatest
common divisor and least common multiple rule for tensor packets. Regular finite field characters produce
primitive cuspidal projectors and finite Gauss phases. For wild data, projective intertwiners recover an
alternating commutator form. Its radical free quotient determines a finite Heisenberg representation, and
maximal isotropic averaging gives an exact selector. We prove a restricted one break bridge: an equivariant
symplectic isometry between a declared Galois envelope and a type side quotient induces the Heisenberg
comparison uniquely up to scalar, while one cyclic phase condition removes the remaining ambiguity. Odd
residue characteristic is governed by finite Weil phases. Residue characteristic two requires a quadratic
refinement and its Arf invariant. A matrix holonomy theorem then gives the exact gluing criterion on
a finite transport graph. The general arithmetic packet realization is stated as Conjecture 66. Detailed
ordinary proofs give restricted arithmetic realizations in all odd prime-power ranks and in all dyadic
ranks for the stated increasing-break families. The complete comparison of pair local factors remains a
conditional input for the same arithmetic candidate.

1 Introduction

The local Langlands correspondence for GLn(K) is an established theorem. It matches irreducible
smooth representations of GLn(K) with Frobenius semisimple Weil Deligne representations of
dimension n. Its proof and normalization draw on global methods, harmonic analysis, types, local
factors, and the geometry of Shimura varieties [19, 17, 8]. This chapter asks a narrower structural
question. Which parts of the local correspondence admit finite packet coordinates whose projectors,
transfers, phases, and gluing laws can be proved directly?
  The answer has a sharp division. The tame layers are explicit. A tame irreducible Weil representation
is induced from a character of an unramified extension. Its inertia restriction is one Frobenius orbit.
Regular characters of elliptic finite field tori give cuspidal blocks through the Deligne and Lusztig
construction [13]. Their tensor products are controlled by a greatest common divisor and least common
multiple decomposition. The corresponding cycle orientation and finite Gauss phases can be computed
exactly. These features are closely related to the tame lifting and essentially tame correspondence of
Bushnell and Henniart [4, 5, 6, 7, 9].
  Wild data are different. The restriction to wild inertia need not split into cyclic characters. On the
type side, simple character theory produces finite symplectic quotients and Heisenberg representations
[11]. Canonical beta extensions fix a phase ambiguity in the extension to the normalizer [2, 14]. On the
Galois side, higher ramification gives a canonical filtration and strong numerical constraints [10]. The
missing construction is not another finite matrix calculation. It is a choice free passage from an arbitrary
wild inertia atom to a finite symplectic envelope that agrees with the type side quotient.
  We therefore separate three levels of assertion. First, this chapter proves finite algebraic theorems
about tame orbits, Heisenberg groups, twisted group algebras, finite Weil phases, and transport graphs.
Second, it proves a restricted one break bridge once a normal wild datum and an equivariant symplectic
identification are declared. Third, it records the exact additional input needed to pass from that
restricted bridge to an independent construction of all wild atoms.
  The finite Heisenberg theory used here is classical. We use the Stone von Neumann theorem, finite
Weil representations, and standard projective representation theory [15, 25, 26, 22, 16]. The contribution
is the way these results are arranged into one comparison diagram and the matrix holonomy theorem
that controls finite gluing. In residue characteristic two, the alternating form does not determine the
phase. A quadratic refinement and its Arf invariant are required. The underlying quadratic form theory
is standard [24].
  Local factors provide the final test. Henniart showed that pair epsilon factors characterize the local
correspondence in the required range [18]. The tame packet calculations below recover exact local
polynomials and finite Gauss phases for the declared tame atoms. They do not supply the complete
pair factor comparison for arbitrary wild atoms. This boundary is retained throughout this chapter.
  Arithmetic realization and identification of an actual candidate are separate problems. The
realization endpoint is conjecture 66. The restricted constructions are developed in section 19 and
the detailed construction appendices. They have ordinary mathematical proofs with retained internal
reviews. Their formal coverage is stated separately in the formal companion.

An atom, its finite packet data, and its arithmetic realization have different roles.

A Weil atom is an irreducible Weil representation. A finite packet records selected quotient spaces,
projectors, central extensions, phases, and transports. An arithmetic realization is an actual admissible
representation of the required general linear group together with a comparison and recovery of that

1 Introduction

Automorphy lifting joins several kinds of mathematics that are easy to conflate. A residual
representation must first occur in an automorphic carrier. The chosen characteristic zero representation
must lie on a deformation problem controlled by local conditions. A patching argument must show
that the automorphic module reaches the relevant part of the deformation space. A comparison such as
R ∼= T must identify the arithmetic and Hecke coordinates. Finally, the resulting Hecke point must be
classical and must carry the expected Galois representation with the required local compatibility.
  None of these steps is merely a change of notation. A deeper lift above one residual representation
cannot create a missing residual companion. Freeness over an auxiliary group algebra does not imply
that every component of a deformation ring is occupied. An isomorphism of rings transports support
that already exists, but it does not create a nonzero automorphic vector. A nonzero class in completed
or torsion cohomology need not be classical without a theorem that says so.
  The Taylor Wiles method and its later forms solve these problems in many important settings
[27, 24, 9, 14, 12]. Higher dimensional and derived versions use a broader range of local deformation
rings, residual image conditions, torsion classes, and cohomological carriers [8, 3, 6, 25, 17, 22, 7, 19].
